what: The score is the fixed-position insertion increase minus the customer's singleton-route cost: Δ(i,c,j) - 2·d(depot,c). Thus lower scores correspond to larger depot-travel savings from consolidating the customer into the current route. It uses only distance-matrix lookups and runs in O(1) time per call.
why: Because new routes are seeded with farthest customers, plain cheapest insertion can postpone other expensive-to-serve customers in favor of locally cheap but low-value insertions. This Clarke–Wright-like net-saving score favors customers that are both geometrically compatible with the current route and costly to leave for another depot-based route. It has no tuned instance-specific constants, and intra-route 2-opt can later improve the resulting order. Its main limitation is that it ignores demand-packing opportunities and interactions among unassigned customers, so heterogeneous demands can still lead to capacity waste; no empirical improvement is claimed.
